title: The Villa and the Corolla: Granville, the Ruined Fortune, and Thirty Avenue Montaigne
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Granville, the birth above the Channel
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: On the twenty-first of January 1905, in a pink and grey villa called Les Rhumbs on a clifftop above the Channel, Madeleine Dior gives birth to the second of her five children. His father Maurice manufactures fertilizer through the port below, and the money is new and ample. The house takes the weather full in the face; its garden is walled against the sea and planted anyway. A century on, the villa carries his name over the door, the only museum in France given to one couturier.
stops.quote: The most important feature of my life – I would be both ungrateful and untruthful if I failed to acknowledge it immediately – has been my good luck; and I must also acknowledge my debt to the fortune-tellers who have predicted it.
stops.quote_source: Dior by Dior: The Autobiography of Christian Dior, trans. Antonia Fraser (1957), opening lines
suggested_refs: Villa Les Rhumbs, Granville, now the Musee Christian Dior

stops.name: Granville, the mother's garden
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the garden is dated only to a spread of years, c. 1906 to the 1920s
stops.campa: Madeleine Dior plants an English garden on the seaward side of the villa: roses in beds, lily of the valley under the hedge, a pergola, a compass rose set into the ground where the lawn breaks toward the cliff. Her son helps choose from the seed catalogues and reads the colour plates the way other boys read timetables. Roses and lily of the valley will run through fifty years of his couture, his perfumes, and his jewellery, and he will carry a dried sprig of muguet in a reliquary in his pocket to the end. The garden outlives the fortune that paid for it.
suggested_refs: The restored gardens of the Villa Les Rhumbs, planted by Madeleine Dior

stops.name: Passy, the family moves to Paris
stops.date_confidence: attested year in the standard chronology, 1910 in one museum-derived summary; the street and number of the apartment are not recorded in any source consulted
stops.campa: The family takes an apartment in Passy, on the western edge of Paris, and keeps Granville for the summers. The city gives the boy the second half of his education in looking: shopfronts, the theatre, the costume balls his mother's circle throws, the drawing rooms of 1910 whose grey and white he will paint onto his own salon thirty-five years later. The museum at Granville credits both settings with his first tastes in the matter, the villa on the cliff and the flat in Paris. Which street the flat stood on, nobody consulted here records.
suggested_refs: The Passy quarter of the 16th arrondissement, the Diors' Paris ground from 1911
sources: Musee Christian Dior official biography page

stops.name: Lycee Janson-de-Sailly, the diplomat they intend
stops.date_confidence: attested year; the month is inferred from the ordinary calendar of the baccalaureate
stops.campa: He finishes his secondary education at the Lycee Janson-de-Sailly on the rue de la Pompe, ten minutes on foot from the apartment. His parents intend a diplomat. He intends, without ever saying it loudly enough to be argued with, an architect or a painter. The compromise reached inside the family is that he may draw as much as he likes provided he also studies something serious. Twenty-one years later the Gestapo will interrogate his sister in a house four hundred metres further up the same street.
suggested_refs: Lycee Janson-de-Sailly, 106 rue de la Pompe, Paris 16e

stops.name: Rue Saint-Guillaume, political science against his will
stops.date_confidence: attested years, 1923 to 1926; the month of enrolment is inferred from the academic calendar
stops.campa: At his father's insistence he enrols at the Ecole Libre des Sciences Politiques on the rue Saint-Guillaume, aimed squarely at the foreign service. He attends three years and takes no degree. The arguments at home end in slammed doors and in the worst word he can find for his father. He leaves in 1926 with no qualification and no trade, still drawing an allowance from the fertilizer works. Sciences Po now lists him among the alumni who took an unexpected road.
stops.quote: I used to have frequent arguments with my father which ended in doors slamming and the ultimate expletive 'Filthy bourgeois'
stops.quote_source: Christian Dior, quoted in Marie France Pochna, Christian Dior: The Man Who Made the World Look New (1996), p. 51
suggested_refs: Sciences Po, 27 rue Saint-Guillaume, and its alumni notices concerning Dior

stops.name: Rue La Boetie, the gallery without his name
stops.date_confidence: attested year; no month recorded
stops.campa: Maurice Dior finances his son's art gallery on one condition, that the family name must not appear on the sign; fertilizer money does not associate itself with pictures. So it opens as the Galerie Jacques Bonjean, at 34 rue La Boetie, in the street where Paris sells modern painting. Dior and his friend hang Picasso, Dali, Braque, Max Jacob, Giacometti, Christian Berard. He is twenty-three, and the trade he has found is choosing pictures rather than making them.
suggested_refs: Galerie Jacques Bonjean, 34 rue La Boetie, Paris 8e

stops.name: Granville, the fertilizer fortune ends
stops.date_confidence: attested year for the collapse and the deaths; no month recorded
stops.campa: The Depression takes the fertilizer business, and property speculation finishes what the crash begins. The villa above the sea is sold; the town of Granville will buy it in 1938 for the sake of the garden. Madeleine Dior is dead by now, and one of Christian's brothers with her. The son who had a gallery on his father's money now has neither a father with money nor a gallery. He says afterwards that his mother wasted away in secret and died of grief, and that her death marked him for life.
stops.quote: My mother whom I adored, secretly wasted away and died of grief...; her death...marked me for life.
stops.quote_source: Christian Dior, quoted in Marie France Pochna, Christian Dior: The Man Who Made the World Look New (1996), p. 48; ellipses as transcribed
suggested_refs: The 1938 municipal purchase of the Villa Les Rhumbs by the town of Granville

stops.name: Rue Cambaceres, the second gallery with Pierre Colle
stops.date_confidence: contradiction unresolved: one strand of the record dates the move 1931, immediately on the closure of the Bonjean gallery, another dates it 1932; 1931 is adopted here and the month is not recorded
stops.campa: With the Bonjean gallery gone, Dior joins Pierre Colle at 29 rue Cambaceres on the Right Bank, a quarter of a mile from the first address, and keeps going. The new house shows the Surrealists. It is the last time he will handle other people's work as his own trade. One account of the gallery calls the site an alley connecting the two streets; the two streets are two hundred and fifty metres apart and no named passage joins them in anything consulted here, so the detail is set aside rather than repeated.
suggested_refs: Galerie Pierre Colle, 29 rue Cambaceres, Paris 8e

stops.name: Rue Cambaceres, the doors close
stops.date_confidence: attested to the end of the year; the day is not recorded
stops.campa: The money runs out and the Colle gallery shuts at the end of the year. Dior is twenty-eight, with no capital, no profession, and a family that has none either. What follows is the blank stretch of the life: illness, the south, and no address anybody wrote down properly. He has spent five years learning how to look at a picture and how to price it. He has learned nothing yet that a house will pay him a wage for, and the next thing that happens to him is not a decision but a lung.
suggested_refs: The closure of the Galerie Pierre Colle, end of 1933

stops.name: Callian, the year of the lung
stops.date_confidence: contradiction unresolved: the illness is dated 1933 in the source cited for the gallery closure and 1934 in the chronology followed here; the place is also disputed, Callian in some accounts and Ibiza and the Balearics in others
stops.campa: He falls ill, and most accounts name the illness tuberculosis. He goes south. The family have land at Callian in the Var, a hill village under the Esterel, and he convalesces there, and by other biographies in Ibiza and the Balearics as well. He is out of Paris for roughly a year. He comes back having decided that the trade he will learn is clothes, which is the first decision of his life that his father did not pay for and did not oppose, because his father no longer has the means to do either.
suggested_refs: The Dior family land at Callian, Var

stops.name: Paris, sketches sold by the sheet
stops.date_confidence: attested from 1935; no office or studio address of his own is recorded, because there was none
stops.campa: Back in Paris with nothing, Dior sells fashion drawings by the sheet: to Le Figaro, to Le Jardin des Modes, and straight to the houses. Robert Piguet buys from him, and Patou, Nina Ricci, Maggy Rouff, Molyneux, Schiaparelli, Balenciaga. He is learning the trade from the drawing board rather than from the workroom floor, which is the wrong way round, and he will hold it against himself for twenty years. The pin, the toile, the fitting, the hands of the premiere: all of that is still on the other side of a door.
suggested_refs: Dior's fashion illustrations for Le Figaro and Le Jardin des Modes, 1935-1938

stops.name: Rond-Point des Champs-Elysees, Robert Piguet takes him on
stops.date_confidence: attested year; no month recorded
stops.campa: Robert Piguet, at the Rond-Point des Champs-Elysees, hires him as a design assistant. It is his first position inside a couture house and he is thirty-three years old. Piguet teaches him subtraction: elegance is what is left when the excess has been taken out. Dior designs for three of his collections. He will name Piguet whenever he is asked who taught him, and the lesson holds even inside the collections that made his name a byword for extravagance.
suggested_refs: Maison Robert Piguet, 3 Rond-Point des Champs-Elysees

stops.name: France, the 47th Infantry Division
stops.date_confidence: attested that he was mobilized at the outbreak of war; the garrison, the sector, and the months in uniform are absent from every source consulted, and the pin here is the canonical Paris coordinate standing in for an unknown posting
stops.campa: War is declared and Dior is called up into the 47th Infantry Division. The garrison town, the sector and the months in uniform are absent from everything reached here, and the gap is left open rather than filled with a plausible camp. He is thirty-four, a fashion illustrator with three collections behind him and a year and a half inside a couture house, and for the length of the drole de guerre he is a soldier of a country that is about to stop existing in the form he was born into.
suggested_refs: Service records of the French 47th Infantry Division, 1939-1940

stops.name: Callian, the vegetable years
stops.date_confidence: attested year; the month is inferred from the armistice of June 1940
stops.campa: Demobilized after the armistice, Dior goes back to the family land at Callian and works it. He hoes beside his father, who is old and ruined, and in some accounts sells vegetables to get through. The village under the Esterel has now caught him twice, once sick at twenty-eight and once beaten at thirty-five. It will catch him a third time and keep him: he is buried in its cemetery, a few hundred metres from the ground he is turning over in the summer of 1940.
suggested_refs: The Dior family property at Callian during the 1940 exodus

stops.name: Avenue Matignon, engaged by Lucien Lelong
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the engagement; the departure in 1946 is attested to the year
stops.campa: On the sixth of October 1941 Lucien Lelong engages Dior as a house designer at 16 avenue Matignon; Pierre Balmain follows on the first of December. Lelong, president of the Chambre Syndicale, is at that moment negotiating with the occupying authorities to keep Paris couture in Paris rather than see it moved to Berlin and Vienna and its workers conscripted into German factories. The houses that stay open dress the wives of German officers and of collaborators. Dior cuts for them for five years. Hubert de Givenchy, often placed in this room, does not arrive until 1946, as Dior is leaving.
suggested_refs: Maison Lucien Lelong, 16 avenue Matignon, Paris 8e
Records of the Chambre Syndicale de la Haute Couture Parisienne under the Occupation
sources: Forbes, 'Lucien Lelong: Christian Dior's Mentor Before The New Look'

stops.name: Paris, costumes for Le lit a colonnes
stops.date_confidence: attested year of the film; no shooting or fitting address recorded
stops.campa: Dior begins designing for the cinema, starting with Le lit a colonnes. Costume is the one department of the trade where a garment must read at a distance, in one shot, under lights, and he takes to it immediately. Between the film work and the Lelong ateliers he passes the Occupation employed, fed, and in Paris. His sister, eleven years younger, is at the same date carrying messages for a network that will cost her everything she owns except her life, and he does not know the half of what she is doing.
suggested_refs: Le lit a colonnes (1942), Dior's first film costume credit

stops.name: 180 rue de la Pompe, the sister arrested
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: Catherine Dior has been with the F2 network since November 1941. On the sixth of July 1944 she is arrested in Paris with twenty-six others and taken to 180 rue de la Pompe, the address worked from by the French Gestapo unit known as the bande de la rue de la Pompe, four hundred metres up the street from the lycee where her brother took his baccalaureate. She is interrogated there and tortured there. She gives them nothing. Her brother has money and contacts and a house that dresses German wives, and he cannot get her out.
suggested_refs: 180 rue de la Pompe, Paris 16e, seat of the bande de la rue de la Pompe
sources: The Daily Beast, 'Catherine Dior, Christian's Sister, Was a French Resistance Hero'

stops.name: Ravensbruck, the deportation
stops.date_confidence: attested that she was deported by 15 August 1944; the onward transfers and the liberation date of 19 April 1945 are attested
stops.campa: By the fifteenth of August 1944 Catherine Dior is deported to Ravensbruck, and from there to Torgau, to Abteroda, and to the aircraft factory at Leipzig-Markkleeberg. American troops free her near Dresden on the nineteenth of April 1945 and she is back in Paris on the twenty-eighth of May. She weighs almost nothing. Her brother's first perfume will be called Miss Dior; the house has never confirmed that she is the Miss in question, and the story is repeated everywhere regardless.
suggested_refs: Ravensbruck concentration camp and the Leipzig-Markkleeberg satellite works
sources: History.com, 'Sister, WWII Spy, Muse: Who Was the Real Miss Dior?'

stops.name: Rue du Faubourg Saint-Honore, the star on the pavement
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the star is house legend, told by Dior's own maison about itself and recorded in no contemporary document, and one retelling moves it to the rue Saint-Honore, a different street
stops.campa: On his way to the meeting where the textile magnate Marcel Boussac will offer to finance a couture house under his own name, Dior stops on the rue du Faubourg Saint-Honore because there is a star of cast iron lying loose on the pavement. He picks it up and keeps it. He already carries a four-leaf clover, two hearts, pieces of wood, and dried lily of the valley in a reliquary, and he consults a clairvoyant, Madame Delahaye, before large decisions. The house tells this story about itself. Nothing outside the house records it.
suggested_refs: La Galerie Dior, house mini-story 'The star'
The dress named Etoile, Haute Couture Spring-Summer 1952
sources: ICON-ICON, 'The Clover, Lily of the Valley, Star and Bee'

stops.name: 30 Avenue Montaigne, the house opens
stops.date_confidence: contradiction unresolved: 8 October 1946 is given as the founding and 16 December 1946 as the physical opening of the doors; both circulate as the date the house began
stops.campa: The Maison Christian Dior opens at 30 avenue Montaigne on Boussac's textile money: about eighty-five staff and seven fit models under one roof. Dior is forty-one and has never run anything. He says afterwards that the first thing he had to make was not a dress but a character, Christian Dior the couturier, because otherwise he could not stop feeling like an amateur among people who had been at this since they were fourteen. Cristobal Balenciaga has been working ten minutes away on the avenue George V since 1937.
stops.quote: Having entered very late into this profession where others had spent a lifetime learning, and having had no training to guide me except my own instincts, I had always been afraid of betraying my ignorance of it. Perhaps it was this very fear of remaining the perpetual amateur that spurred me on to brush aside my doubts at last, and invent the character of Christian Dior, couturier.
stops.quote_source: Dior by Dior: The Autobiography of Christian Dior, trans. Antonia Fraser (1957)
suggested_refs: 30 avenue Montaigne, Paris 8e, the house's original and permanent address

stops.name: 30 Avenue Montaigne, the Corolle line
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: Ninety garments: rounded shoulder, waist pulled in, skirt thrown out over yards of cloth that seven years of rationing had made unthinkable. He calls the line Corolle, after the ring of petals around a flower's centre. Carmel Snow of Harper's Bazaar, sitting in the salon, tells him it is a revolution and that his dresses have such a new look, and the phrase leaves the room and never comes back to him. Cristobal Balenciaga will spend the next decade taking this silhouette apart, and in 1951 will remove the waist from it altogether.
stops.quote: It is quite a revolution, dear Christian. Your dresses have such a new look. They are quite wonderful you know.
stops.quote_source: Carmel Snow, quoted in Marie France Pochna, Christian Dior: The Man Who Made the World Look New (Arcade, 1996), p. 135
suggested_refs: The Corolle collection, 12 February 1947, and the surviving Bar suit
sources: WWD, 'How Christian Dior Revolutionized Fashion With His New Look'

stops.name: Hotel Ritz, Eva Peron in the salon
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: Eva Peron, days after France hangs the Legion of Honour on her, receives couturiers in her suite at the Ritz on the place Vendome. Dior sends gowns; so do Fath and Rochas. Paris is five months into the New Look and two years out of the Occupation, and the city is selling silhouettes to a continent that has not eaten properly since 1940. Marcel Proust worked this same hotel at impossible hours thirty years earlier, buying Faubourg Saint-Germain gossip off the maitre d'hotel. The Ritz keeps handing the atlas the same address.
suggested_refs: Hotel Ritz, place Vendome, Paris, and Eva Peron's 1947 European tour

stops.name: Dallas, the Neiman Marcus award
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month
stops.campa: Dior crosses the Atlantic for the first time to take the Neiman Marcus Award for Distinguished Service in the Field of Fashion from Stanley Marcus, honoured the same year as Salvatore Ferragamo and Norman Hartnell. Eight months after his first collection, a Paris couturier is being decorated in Texas. Within a year his designs are reported to account for about three quarters of French fashion export revenue, a figure that circulates constantly and that no audited source consulted here supports.
stops.quote: To reach Dallas, Texas, I had to cross the ocean and enter the New World.
stops.quote_source: Christian Dior at the Neiman Marcus Award ceremony, Dallas, September 1947
suggested_refs: The Neiman Marcus flagship, 1618 Main Street, Dallas
sources: WWD, 'Memories of the Neiman Marcus Award'

stops.name: Paris, the perfume named for the sister
stops.date_confidence: attested year; the month is not fixed in the sources consulted, and the attribution of the name to Catherine Dior is traditional and has never been confirmed by the house
stops.campa: The house launches its first perfume, Miss Dior, and opens the Colifichets boutique for accessories in the same year. A couture house that sells scent and gloves as well as dresses is a different animal from one that sells only dresses, and 1947 is the year Dior becomes the first of the two. The name is said everywhere to honour Catherine, two years back from Ravensbruck. The house has never said so, and the claim rests on repetition rather than on any statement from the family or from Christian himself.
suggested_refs: Miss Dior, 1947, and the Colifichets boutique at avenue Montaigne
sources: History.com, 'Who Was the Real Miss Dior?'

stops.name: East 57th Street, the New York house
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month; the identification of the address as 21 East 57th Street is carried from secondary sources and tagged as reconstruction
stops.campa: A second house opens on East 57th Street off Fifth Avenue, the first permanent American ground the maison holds, selling ready-to-wear cut for a market the Paris ateliers cannot dress one body at a time. The following year Dior tours the United States and finds the Anti-Trust Division of the Department of Justice reading his licensing and export contracts. He has built in three years a thing American law recognises before French fashion writing does. It is not a couturier. It is a distribution system with a couturier inside it.
suggested_refs: Christian Dior New York, 21 East 57th Street

stops.name: Paris, the Legion of Honour
stops.date_confidence: attested year; no month recorded
stops.campa: France gives Dior the Legion of Honour. Three years earlier the same decoration went to Eva Peron in the same city; eight years later it will go to Cristobal Balenciaga. The state is now underwriting couture as a national export and Dior is the reason it can: his house is the largest single earner in a trade France counts beside wine and aircraft. In 1952 the New York Times will put the maison's gross annual income at about seventeen million dollars, a figure reported rather than audited.
suggested_refs: Dior's Legion of Honour, 1950
New York Times reporting on the maison's revenues, 1952
sources: WWD timeline citing the New York Times

stops.name: Montauroux, the chateau bought back
stops.date_confidence: contradiction unresolved: the purchase is dated 1950 in some accounts and 1951 in others, and one summary leaves the year open; the building is called eighteenth-century in one description and nineteenth-century in another
stops.campa: Dior buys a ruined chateau at Montauroux, five kilometres across the valley from the Callian land where he hoed vegetables in 1940. La Colle Noire is the house he means to retire into, and he restores it slowly, with the roses and the lavender he grew up among and the water he pipes down himself. He is the son of a man ruined by property, buying property back in the country his family lost. He will own it six years and spend very little time inside it.
suggested_refs: Chateau de la Colle Noire, Montauroux, Var

stops.name: Palazzo Labia, the Bal Oriental
stops.date_confidence: unverified: the ball is securely dated to September 1951, the day here is approximate, and Dior's participation is carried from general fashion-historical accounts that were not re-checked in the research pass behind this file
stops.campa: Carlos de Beistegui throws the Bal Oriental at the Palazzo Labia and half of Europe comes dressed by Paris. Dior makes costumes for it, under Tiepolo's frescoes of Antony and Cleopatra, in a city that has not staged anything on this scale since the Republic fell. The New Look is four years old and is now the uniform of a class that thought it had been abolished in 1945. This item was not independently re-checked and is carried flagged rather than dropped.
suggested_refs: The Beistegui Ball, Palazzo Labia, Venice, September 1951
sources: General accounts of the 1951 Beistegui Ball, not verified in this research pass

stops.name: London and Caracas, the name goes out on licence
stops.date_confidence: attested year; no street address for the London company or the Caracas boutique appears in any source consulted, and the London pin here is the city centre standing in for an unknown address
stops.campa: C.D. Models Ltd begins producing a licensed Dior line in London, and a licensed boutique opens in Caracas. Neither address is recorded anywhere consulted. Six years after the first collection the name is manufacturing on two continents under other people's roofs, and the licence, not the dress, is the invention that will outlive him. Ten years after his death Roland Barthes will publish Systeme de la mode and take apart the written language by which exactly this machine sells.
suggested_refs: C.D. Models Ltd, London
The Dior licensing structure of the early 1950s

stops.name: Paris, Roger Vivier and the heel
stops.date_confidence: attested year; no month recorded
stops.campa: Dior brings in the shoemakers Herman Delman and Roger Vivier. Vivier cuts a heel the way a couturier cuts a bodice and works under the Dior name rather than his own, which is the first time a Paris house has put another designer's craft inside its own label and kept the label. The silhouette is now complete from the floor upward and the house sells the whole of it: the shoe, the stocking, the skirt, the scent, and the idea that these are one object.
suggested_refs: Roger Vivier's shoes for Christian Dior, 1953-1963

stops.name: Paris, the dictionary of fashion
stops.date_confidence: attested year of publication; no month recorded
stops.campa: Dior publishes The Little Dictionary of Fashion, an alphabet of the trade written for women who will never buy couture: how to wear a scarf, what to do about a thick waist, why black is not automatically elegant. It opens by observing that no couturier has ever tried to compile a dictionary. The man writing it left Sciences Po without a degree, learned his trade selling drawings by the sheet, and has now produced the reference book that the trained ones did not think to write.
stops.quote: Much has been written about fashion, in all its aspects, but I do not think any couturier has ever before attempted to compile a dictionary on the subject.
stops.quote_source: Christian Dior, The Little Dictionary of Fashion (1954), opening line
suggested_refs: Christian Dior, The Little Dictionary of Fashion (1954; V&A reprint 2007)

stops.name: 30 Avenue Montaigne, the H-Line
stops.date_confidence: attested year; the month is inferred from the ordinary autumn-collection calendar
stops.campa: The H-Line flattens the bust and drops the waist, and the press and the public turn on him. Seven years after he put the waist back at the centre of the female body he takes it away again, and is accused of it as of a betrayal, as though the body under the cloth were public property and he had signed something. He answers, when he is asked anything at all, that the great secret of haute couture is that a well-cut dress is the dress which contains the least cuts. The controversy sells the collection.
stops.quote: It is one of the great secrets of haute couture that a well-cut dress is the dress which contains the least cuts.
stops.quote_source: Dior by Dior: The Autobiography of Christian Dior, trans. Antonia Fraser, c. p. 77
suggested_refs: The H-Line collection, autumn 1954, and the press campaign against it

stops.name: Blenheim Palace, the show under Vanbrugh's ceilings
stops.date_confidence: unverified: dated to November 1954 in general accounts, carried from fashion-historical memory and not independently re-checked in the research pass behind this file
stops.campa: Dior shows a collection inside Blenheim Palace for a charity gala given by the Duke and Duchess of Marlborough, dressing English society under Vanbrugh's baroque ceilings. A Paris couturier holding a show in an English ducal house is a new kind of event in 1954 and becomes an ordinary one afterwards. Like the Venice ball of three years earlier, this item is carried from general accounts rather than from any source opened in this research pass, and it is flagged as such here rather than quietly dropped.
suggested_refs: The 1954 Dior show at Blenheim Palace, Woodstock
sources: General accounts of the 1954 Blenheim Palace Dior show, not verified in this research pass

stops.name: Avenue George V, the master of us all
stops.date_confidence: undated tradition: no contemporary source records Dior saying it, the phrase is known chiefly from the title of Mary Blume's 2013 book on Balenciaga, and the date here is a placement inside the years the two houses overlapped rather than a dating of the words
stops.campa: Ten minutes on foot from avenue Montaigne, Cristobal Balenciaga has worked at 10 avenue George V since 1937. Dior is said to have called him the master of us all, and the sentence has been repeated for seventy years without a document under it; it supplied the title of Mary Blume's book on Balenciaga long afterwards. A second line runs alongside it in the same undocumented register. What is attested is the shape of the rivalry: two houses in one quarter, one adding the waist and one removing it.
stops.quote: with fabrics, we do what we can, Balenciaga does what he wants.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Christian Dior, undated, recorded in cristobal_balenciaga.journey.json alongside a parallel remark of Coco Chanel
suggested_refs: Mary Blume, The Master of Us All: Balenciaga, His Workrooms, His World (2013)
sources: Mary Blume, The Master of Us All

stops.name: 30 Avenue Montaigne, an assistant of eighteen
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the frequent claim that Saint Laurent was twenty-one when hired is false, and conflates his age at hiring with his age when he succeeded Dior in 1957
stops.campa: On the twentieth of June 1955 the house takes on a design assistant of eighteen from Oran, Yves Saint Laurent, born the first of August 1936. Dior sets him to drawing and then to whole passages of collection. Within two years the boy will be running the maison. He is described everywhere as having been twenty-one when he was hired; he was twenty-one when Dior died, and the two ages have been folded into one another so thoroughly that the correction has to be made from his birth certificate each time.
suggested_refs: Yves Saint Laurent's engagement at Dior, 20 June 1955

stops.name: New York, the Parsons award and Diorissimo
stops.date_confidence: attested year for both the award and the fragrance; no months recorded
stops.campa: Parsons School of Design gives Dior its Distinguished Achievement Award in New York, and the house launches Diorissimo, built on lily of the valley: his mother's flower from the garden at Granville and the sprig he carries dried in a reliquary in his pocket. He is fifty-one. He has been a couturier under his own name for nine years and there is no longer anything in the trade that has not been handed to him. He is also, by every account of the last two years, tired.
suggested_refs: Diorissimo, 1956
The Parsons Distinguished Achievement Award

stops.name: Boulevard Jules-Sandeau, the last address
stops.date_confidence: attested to the decade; the year of the move and the month are not recorded in any source consulted
stops.campa: Dior keeps his Paris residence at 7 boulevard Jules-Sandeau in the sixteenth arrondissement: a few streets from the Passy apartment his parents took in 1911, a few more from the lycee, and closer still to the house on the rue de la Pompe where his sister was interrogated. A man who crosses the Atlantic for his trade has ended his life inside one square kilometre of his own childhood. What year he took the flat, nobody consulted here says, and the sources give only the decade.
suggested_refs: 7 boulevard Jules-Sandeau, Paris 16e

stops.name: New York, the cover of Time
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the cover; the accompanying claim that he was the first fashion designer on a Time cover is false, Elsa Schiaparelli having appeared there on 13 August 1934
stops.campa: Time puts Dior on its cover on the fourth of March 1957. He is often called the first fashion designer to appear there and he is not: Elsa Schiaparelli was on the cover of the thirteenth of August 1934, twenty-two years and seven months before him. What is true without the embellishment is that an American newsweekly has decided a French dressmaker is general news, which it had also decided in 1934, and which in the twenty-two years between it did not decide once.
suggested_refs: Time magazine cover, 4 March 1957
Time magazine cover, 13 August 1934, Elsa Schiaparelli

stops.name: Montecatini Terme, the third heart attack
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the cause is genuinely disputed rather than merely undocumented, and the two lenses of this record even give the spa hotel two slightly different coordinate pairs
stops.campa: Dior goes to take the waters at Montecatini Terme in Tuscany and dies there of a heart attack, reportedly his third, at fifty-two. What set it off is disputed rather than unrecorded: a heavy card game, a fish bone at dinner, or, in the version Paris society passed around and Baron de Rede wrote into his memoirs, a strenuous private encounter. The house says heart attack and stops there. Eleven years of couture under his own name end in a spa hotel out of season.
suggested_refs: Grand Hotel et de la Pace, Montecatini Terme
sources: Musee Yves Saint Laurent Paris, 'Death of Christian Dior'
Nicki Swift, 'The Truth About Christian Dior's Mysterious Death'

stops.name: Saint-Honore d'Eylau, nine thousand mourners
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month; the day is not fixed in any source consulted, and the parish has since moved, so the 1957 church is the older building on the place Victor-Hugo and not the avenue Raymond-Poincare church that replaced it in 1974
stops.campa: Paris buries him from Saint-Honore d'Eylau on the place Victor-Hugo, the parish church of the quarter he lived in and the quarter he grew up in. An estimated nine thousand people come. The coffin is covered in lily of the valley, his mother's flower and his own. The couture houses of the city are said to have shut for the day. Which day in late October the funeral fell on is not fixed anywhere consulted, which is a strange gap for an event that size and is left standing as a gap.
suggested_refs: Eglise Saint-Honore d'Eylau, place Victor-Hugo, Paris 16e

stops.name: Callian, the grave by the chapel
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month; the day is inferred, and one automated summary of the record names the Chateau de la Colle Noire as the burial place instead, a contradiction recorded here rather than resolved
stops.campa: He is buried in the small cemetery at Callian, near the chapel of Saint-Barthelemy, beside his father, and later beside his housekeeper and beside Catherine, who dies in the village in 2008. The place that took him in sick at twenty-eight and broke at thirty-five keeps him. One summary of the record puts the grave at La Colle Noire instead; photographs of the actual stone at Callian outweigh it, and the disagreement is written down rather than tidied away.
suggested_refs: The Dior family grave, cimetiere de Callian, Var
sources: Alamy, Getty and Bridgeman photograph captions of the Callian grave

stops.name: 30 Avenue Montaigne, the successor aged twenty-one
stops.date_confidence: attested year; the day and month of the appointment are not fixed in the sources consulted, and Dior's reported private wish that Saint Laurent should succeed him is traditional and rests on no document
stops.campa: Yves Saint Laurent, twenty-one, is named head designer of the House of Dior. Dior is reported to have told associates that the boy should take it if anything happened to him; the report is traditional and no document carries it. The house does not close, which in 1957 is not the obvious outcome: a maison built on one man's eye and one man's name had never before survived that man. Boussac's money and the licensing structure carry it through, and the name detaches from the body that owned it.
suggested_refs: Yves Saint Laurent's first Dior collection, Trapeze, spring 1958

stops.name: Granville, the villa becomes a museum
stops.date_confidence: attested year of the museum's opening; the 1906 purchase by his parents and the 1938 municipal acquisition are attested
stops.campa: The Villa Les Rhumbs, bought by Dior's parents in 1906 and sold off after the crash, acquired by the town of Granville in 1938 for the sake of the garden, opens as the Musee Christian Dior. It is the only museum in France carrying the Musee de France label and given over to a single couturier. A statue of him stands in the grounds near the compass rose, facing the Channel that his mother's roses were planted against and that the wind still comes off in walls.
suggested_refs: Musee Christian Dior, Villa Les Rhumbs, Granville

stops.name: Victoria and Albert Museum, Designer of Dreams
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the opening; the run closed 1 September 2019
stops.campa: Christian Dior: Designer of Dreams opens at the Victoria and Albert Museum, curated by Oriole Cullen and designed by Nathalie Criniere: about five hundred objects, two hundred of them haute couture. It runs seven months and draws 594,994 visitors, the most-visited exhibition in the museum's history, past Alexander McQueen's Savage Beauty by more than a hundred thousand. Sixty-two years after his death the dresses pull larger crowds than they did while there was a man inside the house cutting them.
suggested_refs: Christian Dior: Designer of Dreams, V&A, 2 February to 1 September 2019
sources: The Art Newspaper, 'Dior show smashes total attendance record at the V&A'
